headline: Maria Makeenkova, Ataberk Olgun and co-authors let a DDR5 memory controller delay a RowHammer preventive refresh behind ordinary requests that do not touch the hammered row, and measure a 21.7 percent average speedup for the four most refresh-hungry mitigations.

items.title: A less dense nitride traps on the dangling bonds it already has
items.dek: Jonathon Cottom and Emilia Olsson varied the density of amorphous silicon nitride — the insulator that stores the charge in 3D NAND flash — and found that the looser film's extra internal void surface shifts electron capture onto silicon dangling bonds that exist before any electron arrives.
items.why_it_matters: This brief covered the same pair's trap taxonomy on 6 October, where the finding was that the deepest traps are created by the electron that gets caught; density is the knob that was missing. Plasma power and pressure set the density of a deposited nitride, so the process engineer's lever now changes which of three capture routes dominates, not merely how many traps the film contains. The three routes sit at different depths, so moving the mixture moves the retention distribution even when the total trap count does not.
items.background_md: Amorphous silicon nitride stores a bit as electrons parked in localised states inside the insulator, and how far those states sit below the mobility edge — the energy above which a carrier moves freely through a disordered solid — decides how long the bit survives, because emptying a trap is thermally activated over that depth. The network supplying those states is not fully dense: an amorphous film contains internal void space, and the silicon atoms lining a void have fewer neighbours than atoms in the bulk. Mass density is one of the few deposition parameters that moves that void fraction directly.
items.deeper_md:
The comparison is 2.92 against 3.15 g/cm³, inside a 2.86–3.19 g/cm³ range, over 499 stoichiometric Si₁₂₀N₁₆₀ cells — 415 from the pair's own October set plus 84 from Hückmann and co-workers — of which 496 enter the three-route analysis. Accessible void fraction rises from 8.4 % at 3.15 g/cm³ to 12.6 % at 2.92 g/cm³; crystalline α-Si₃N₄ measures 7.8 % by the same definition. The supply of free three-coordinate silicon precursors more than triples, and the mixture follows: capture at pre-existing K centres goes from 9 % to 29 %, charge-induced K formation falls from 45 % to 34 %, and polaronic trapping from 46 % to 37 %. Reported depths below the mobility edge are about 3.25 eV (pre-existing K), 3.34 eV (induced K) and 2.87 eV (polaronic), with relaxation energies near 1.4, 1.5 and 1.2 eV, and those depths stay put across the density range — only the proportions move.

The caveats are the ones that limited the 6 October item: 0 K hybrid-functional calculations on hydrogen-free cells in a single −1 charge state, with the route assignment inferred from a neutral-film structural fingerprint rather than measured. Nobody has published a contrary density dependence; the honest statement is that nobody has published a measured one either.

glossary.definition: A silicon atom in silicon nitride bonded to only three nitrogens, leaving one unpaired electron on a dangling bond; it is the canonical deep electron trap in the material.
The share of an amorphous film's volume that a probe of a given size can reach — the internal pore space, as distinct from the free volume between atoms in a dense network.
Capture in which no bond breaks: the arriving electron localises and the surrounding lattice relaxes around it, and that relaxation is what holds the carrier in place.
In a disordered solid there is no sharp band edge; the mobility edge is the energy above which states are extended enough to carry current, and trap depths are quoted below it.

items.fab_angle: Nitride density is not something a teaching fab measures directly, but refractive index tracks it, and an ellipsometer reading on a PECVD nitride is a routine step. If the trapping mixture rather than the trap count is what density controls, then logging the index with every deposition — not just checking it is in spec — is what lets a later retention measurement be attributed to anything.

items.title: Fit the beam's shape from the image's own autocorrelation
items.dek: Rebecca Guan and co-authors focus and de-astigmatise a desktop scanning electron microscope by fitting the beam's shape out of the autocorrelation of the image it just took, instead of scoring each image with a single sharpness number.
items.why_it_matters: A sharpness number tells you an image got better; it does not tell you which aberration was wrong, so correcting astigmatism means searching two stigmator axes blind. An image autocorrelation is the specimen's own autocorrelation convolved with the beam's, so the fitted ellipse separates the two stigmator coefficients from defocus and gives each one a direction to move. That is how a 166-second automated run narrowed the autocorrelation width from 24.6 to 17.8 pixels, and also why the search has to be re-run at the target field width rather than reusing the coarse result.
items.background_md: What a scanning electron microscope records is the specimen convolved with the shape of the electron probe, so every measurement of a feature is really a measurement of feature plus beam. Two things ruin the probe: defocus, which spreads it into a disc, and astigmatism, which stretches it into an ellipse whose orientation follows wherever the lens field is asymmetric. On most instruments both are corrected by hand, by turning knobs until the picture looks right, which makes the correction only as repeatable as the operator and sends it back to zero whenever working distance or magnification changes.
items.deeper_md:
The scoring works because an image is the surface convolved with the point spread function, so the image autocorrelation is the surface autocorrelation convolved with the beam's: a taller, sharper central peak means better focus, an elliptical peak means astigmatism. Working distance is scored by summing the four autocorrelation values adjacent to the centre after Canny edge preprocessing; stigmation is found by fitting the beam autocorrelation to a Zernike pupil model and minimising the fitted astigmatism coefficients. Quality is the x and y full widths at half maximum added in quadrature. Bayesian optimisation drives the search — 50 iterations for working distance at a 104 µm field width, then 50 more at the target width — on a Phenom Pharos G2, a Schottky field-emission desktop instrument rated below 2.0 nm. Autocorrelation FWHM fell from 20.5 to 16.1 pixels on a coin at a 6.22 µm field, 24.6 to 17.8 on a nanoparticle-coated polymer at 4.27 µm, and 38.7 to 28.6 on coarse coin features at 2.86 µm.

The named failure mode is specific and believable: if large topographic features fill the field, the routine optimises the circularity of the sample rather than of the beam. The model also assumes a symmetric, real-valued probe, so only symmetric aberrations are reachable, and the text gives 50 stigmation iterations in one section and 30 in another. Autocorrelation as a sharpness function is not contested — Rudnaya's 2011 thesis already corrected defocus and twofold astigmatism jointly by three-parameter simplex search on one; what is new is fitting a beam shape instead of maximising a scalar.

glossary.definition: An image correlated against shifted copies of itself; the width of the resulting central peak measures the smallest length scale the image actually resolves.
A pair of weak quadrupole coils that apply a deliberate opposing astigmatism to pull an elliptical electron probe back to round; two independent axes, so two numbers to set.
Full width at half maximum — the width of a peak at half its height, used here on the autocorrelation peak so a narrower number means a tighter probe.
The gap between the final lens and the specimen; on a fixed-height desktop column it cannot be moved mechanically, so focus is changed through the lens excitation instead.

items.fab_angle: Any linewidth a club measures on an SEM inherits the operator's stigmation, because an elliptical probe widens a line in one direction and narrows it in the other. A routine that reports the fitted astigmatism coefficients turns that into a logged number per session, which is the difference between a CD measurement you can compare across two weeks and one you cannot.

items.title: Boron nitride is not inert: 0.5 V/nm ionises what is inside it
items.dek: Ilia Begichev and co-authors used a graphene sheet sandwiched between hexagonal boron nitride crystals as its own charge meter, and found that pushing the out-of-plane field past about 0.5 volts per nanometre ionises defects inside the boron nitride and dopes the graphene.
items.why_it_matters: Hexagonal boron nitride is used precisely because it is assumed to do nothing electrically — it is the substrate, the gate dielectric and the encapsulant in most two-dimensional device measurements. If a field those experiments routinely apply is enough to move charge out of the dielectric and into the channel, then part of what gets read as a property of the channel is a property of the crystal around it, and carrier density stops being gate voltage times capacitance.
items.background_md: Hexagonal boron nitride is the standard partner material for two-dimensional electronics: an insulator with a band gap near 6 eV that cleaves into atomically flat flakes with no surface dangling bonds, and sits close enough to graphene's lattice to carry it without scattering carriers. The usual experiment stacks a conducting monolayer between two boron nitride flakes with metal gates outside, and treats the boron nitride purely as a capacitor — charge on the gate, charge in the channel, nothing in between. Real crystals contain point defects, substitutional carbon chief among them, and whether those are electrically active in a working device is a different question from whether spectroscopy can see them.
items.deeper_md:
Graphene is the detector here rather than the subject: its sheet resistance against gate voltage gives carrier density, and the width of the resistance peak gives density inhomogeneity, so charge arriving from the boron nitride shows up as both a shift and a broadening. Beyond a displacement field of roughly 0.5 V/nm the authors report extra electron doping of 10–20 × 10⁹ cm⁻² together with increased inhomogeneity, and attribute both to ionisation of states inside the boron nitride gap. From the doping they infer a bulk defect density of about 1–7 × 10⁻⁵ nm⁻³ that varies between crystals, and that spread is the most useful number in the preprint, because it makes the effect a property of a particular crystal rather than of the material.

Two things to hold lightly. The preprint gives no defect level positions, so which defect is being ionised is not established; carbon substituting for boron is the usual candidate, and a 2021 scanning-tunnelling study of carbon-doped boron nitride found donor-like single-site states plus ladders of mid-gap states from multi-site complexes. A 2025 calculation points the causation the other way — that graphene encapsulation screens the defect and shifts its levels, so the charge state belongs to the stack rather than to the defect, and reorientation barriers are low enough for moderate gate voltages to cross. Neither this preprint nor those papers settles it.

glossary.definition: In a dual-gated stack, the average of the two gate-induced fields; it sets the perpendicular electric field across the layers independently of how much charge is put into the channel.
Burying a conducting monolayer between two insulating flakes so neither face touches air or a dirty substrate; it is the single change that made two-dimensional transport measurements reproducible.
Sheet carrier density — carriers per unit area rather than per unit volume, the natural unit for a conductor one atom thick; 10¹⁰ cm⁻² is a very light doping for graphene.
Spatial variation in local carrier density across a device, read off as broadening of the resistance peak near charge neutrality; it is the standard proxy for how much disorder the channel sees.

items.title: A RowHammer refresh can wait, as long as nobody opens that row
items.dek: Maria Makeenkova and five co-authors rewrote the DDR5 memory controller's request scheduler so a preventive refresh — the extra row refresh a RowHammer defence orders to repair the neighbours a hammered row disturbed — waits its turn instead of jumping the queue.
items.why_it_matters: Read-disturbance defences are the standing tax on DRAM performance, and the whole tax comes from treating the preventive refresh as urgent. The claim here is that urgency was never the requirement: correctness only needs the refresh to land before the aggressor row is opened again, which is a blacklist on one row rather than a priority on one command. That distinction is worth 21.7 percent on the mitigations that issue the most refreshes, and worth nothing at all on the two that barely issue any — so it also measures which existing defences were paying for urgency they did not need.
items.background_md: A DRAM row is a line of capacitors, and opening one row disturbs the charge held in the rows physically beside it; hammer one row often enough and a neighbour's bit flips. The number of activations a row tolerates has fallen with every density generation, so each generation needs a defence that counts activations and refreshes the likely victims before the count gets dangerous. Those extra refreshes travel on the same command bus as real reads and writes, and a row cannot be read while it is being refreshed, which is the entire source of their cost.
items.deeper_md:
The mechanism is a 32-entry content-addressable queue, the PROQ. When a mitigation orders a preventive refresh, the aggressor row's address enters the PROQ and is blacklisted: the FR-FCFS scheduler then serves the oldest ready request that is not for a blacklisted row, with a Request Age Counter keeping demand requests and pending refreshes in a single age order. Nothing is forced to the front until the PROQ reaches 31 of its 32 entries. The paper's own accounting puts the added state at about 170 bytes, though its hardware table also lists 0.72 KB of CAM and 0.058 mm² across six channels, which does not obviously reconcile.

Results come from Ramulator 2.0 with a DDR5 model, two channels and eight cores, over 55 workloads drawn from SPEC CPU2006 and CPU2017, TPC, MediaBench and YCSB. At a threshold of 125 activations the six-mitigation average is 14.5 percent speedup and 14.8 percent DRAM energy saving; restricted to the four refresh-heavy ones it is 21.7 percent and 22.1 percent, led by Hydra at 50.8 percent, while Graphene gains 0.0 percent and ABACuS 0.3 percent because neither issues many refreshes. Across all six techniques and all four thresholds — 125, 250, 500, 1000 — the average falls to 8.6 percent.

Three costs the abstract omits. Reordering forces the mitigation threshold down by twice the blast radius to stay safe; charging DRFM's address-setup activate cuts the average benefit to 11.0 percent; and some workloads show worse 99th-percentile read latency. MICRO 2026 does not meet until 31 October, so nothing public has argued with it yet.

glossary.definition: A refresh issued not on the normal timer but because a mitigation decided a specific row's neighbours are at risk; it occupies the bank for hundreds of nanoseconds and blocks demand traffic to that bank.
The number of times a row can be opened before a neighbouring bit is at risk of flipping; it has fallen by orders of magnitude across DRAM generations and sets how often a mitigation must act.

First-ready, first-come-first-served — the standard DRAM scheduling policy, which prefers requests that hit an already-open row and otherwise takes the oldest, so reordering is already normal behaviour.
How many rows either side of a hammered row can be disturbed by it; it sets how many victims one preventive refresh must cover and how much safety margin reordering costs.

items.title: Emit the leading digit first and ReLU can stop the multiply
items.dek: Yousef Sadegheih, Dorit Merhof and Muhammad Usman built a neural-network accelerator whose multipliers emit their result most-significant digit first, so a ReLU layer — which throws away anything negative — can see a product is negative and abandon the remaining digit cycles.
items.why_it_matters: Almost every efficiency trick in quantised inference buys speed by changing the answer: fewer bits, pruned weights, skipped channels. Digit-order arithmetic buys some of it for nothing — 18.79 percent of digit cycles vanish with the quantised output bit-identical, because the information that the work is wasted arrives before the work is finished. The other 19.6 percent comes from two approximate mechanisms calibrated offline, and those do cost accuracy, 80.58 against 81.20 mean Dice, so the same paper also prices what exactness is worth here.
items.background_md: Ordinary binary multipliers work least-significant digit first, because that is the direction a carry travels; the sign and magnitude of a product are therefore the last things you learn about it. Online arithmetic reverses the order. It represents each digit redundantly — radix-2 digits drawn from −1, 0 and +1 — so a carry never propagates more than one place, and the leading digits of the result can be emitted after a fixed online delay of a few cycles. The price is a sign bit and a magnitude bit per digit instead of one bit, plus a conversion step at the end.
items.deeper_md:
The datapath is a two-stage grouped processing element for signed INT8 operands with in-stream bias accumulation, synthesised at 45 nm and 500 MHz: 0.858 mm² and 0.726 mJ per 192×192 patch for the processing element alone. Four runtime mechanisms watch the digit stream. Two are exact — early negative detection inside ReLU layers, and sign-only decisions in the segmentation head, where only the argmax matters — and together they remove 18.79 percent of digit cycles with the quantised output unchanged. Two are approximate and selected offline under an accuracy constraint: calibrated low-order-digit skipping, and calibrated pruning. None of the four modifies a stored weight. All four together cut digit cycles by 38.38 percent at a mean Dice of 80.58 percent over 73 held-out BraTS cases, against 81.20 percent for the floating-point residual U-Net trained with nnU-Net.

The caveats are about generality rather than correctness. The workload is one segmentation network with ReLU throughout, which is exactly where sign-only decisions pay; a transformer built on GELU and softmax offers far less of that structure. The quoted 16.6 ms latency and 1.67 mJ per patch for an eight-output configuration is a projection, not a measurement. And the preprint names no competing most-significant-digit-first accelerator as a baseline, so the comparison is against its own full-cycle run and a floating-point model, not against the prior art it cites.

glossary.definition: Most-significant-digit-first, or online, arithmetic: operands stream in and results stream out leading digit first, so a downstream stage can start before the upstream one finishes.
The fixed number of input digits that must arrive before the first output digit can be produced; it is a small integer, and it is the latency price paid for left-to-right arithmetic.
One clock step of a digit-serial unit, producing one digit of the result; counting digit cycles rather than operations is how a design like this reports work done.
Twice the overlap between a predicted region and the true region divided by their combined size; the standard score for medical image segmentation, where 1.0 is an exact match.

items.title: A subexponential lattice attack its authors say spares Kyber
items.dek: Yiming Gao, Xuyuan Han and Honggang Hu claim secret-recovery algorithms whose running time grows more slowly than any fixed power of 2 raised to n, for the growing-parameter families behind all seven of NIST's third-round lattice candidates — while stating that Kyber's and Dilithium's standardised parameters are untouched.
items.why_it_matters: A hardness claim about a family of growing parameters and a security level for one fixed parameter set are different statements, and the gap between them is where this result lives. The authors say so themselves, which makes the item the regime assumption rather than the attack: polynomial modulus, polylogarithmically bounded secret and error, and an o(1) sitting in the exponent that no finite dimension can pin down. Nothing deployed changes; what changes is which asymptotic statements can be cited as settled.
items.background_md: The security of lattice cryptography rests on a search problem: given many noisy linear equations modulo q, recover the short secret vector that satisfies them. Hardness gets asserted in two incompatible currencies. Reduction theorems talk about families whose dimension n grows, and state how difficulty must scale with n; a deployed parameter set is a single fixed n with a fixed modulus q, and its security level is an operation count for the best known algorithm at that one size. A theorem in the first currency can be true and still say nothing checkable about the second, because the constants and o(1) terms it hides are exactly what an operation count needs.
items.deeper_md:
The mechanism is a Wagner-style k-list search run with Gaussian sampling. Appending the identity matrix to the public relation makes a guess c for one secret coordinate sᵢ change the squared error norm by exactly (c − sᵢ)², with every other coordinate contributing a common offset, so comparing two candidates isolates one coordinate. Adjacent candidates differ in energy by 2(c − sᵢ) + 1, which says which side of c the secret lies on, so each coordinate costs O(log(2B+1)) comparisons for a coefficient bound B — and one Gaussian list, built over random auxiliary lattices, serves every coordinate and every public label at once. The exponent comes from the list depth: for these families D ≈ ln ln n, and the capacity accumulated over the levels gives log₂N ≈ n/(2D), hence 2^((1/2+o(1))n/ln ln n). NTRU-type quotient relations get a separate affine slice search instead, reaching 2^(O(n/ln ln n)).

The assumptions are where this has to be read. FrodoKEM and SABER require q = n^(κ+o(1)) with κ > 1/2 and Kyber a prime q with κ ≥ 1; Falcon's result covers only quality-qualified keys, and Dilithium's restricts the public relation to a square row block. The paper is a single-version arXiv preprint with no peer review, its authors disclose that AI tools were used in exploration and drafting, and nothing comparable appeared on IACR ePrint the same week. The right reading is a claim awaiting a cryptanalyst, not a result.

glossary.definition: Learning with errors — recover a short secret vector from many linear equations modulo q that each carry a small random error; it is the problem ML-KEM and ML-DSA are built on.
A running time of the form 2^(f(n)) where f grows faster than any logarithm but slower than any constant times n, so it eventually beats every 2^(cn) algorithm without being polynomial.
A term that tends to zero as n grows but whose size at any particular n is unspecified; sitting inside an exponent it can change an operation count by many orders of magnitude.
Solve a sum-to-target problem by splitting it into k lists, merging pairs that agree on part of the target, and recursing; the merge depth is what fixes the list size and hence the runtime.

items.title: Round the optimiser state where it is used, not where it is stored
items.dek: Hanyang Li, Aman Gupta and co-authors show that quantising AdamW's second moment to four bits should round in the space of one over its square root — the quantity that actually divides the update — which closes 70 percent of the validation-loss gap to full-precision AdamW on a 1.4-billion-parameter model.
items.why_it_matters: Every quantiser chooses which of two levels a value snaps to, and the usual choice minimises error in the stored value. AdamW never uses the stored value: it uses one over its square root, a map that is steep near zero, so a small error in the second moment becomes a large error in the next step size. Fixing the rounding space rather than the codebook is what lets 4-bit state track 32-bit training at 2.7 billion parameters, where the existing implementation diverged outright.
items.background_md: Adam and AdamW keep two running averages per parameter: a first moment, the smoothed gradient, and a second moment, the smoothed squared gradient. The second moment is used only through its inverse square root, and that is what makes the optimiser adaptive — a parameter with a history of large gradients takes smaller steps. Two states at 32 bits each is 8 bytes of optimiser memory per parameter, which for a large model exceeds the weights, so the states are the first thing anyone compresses. They also feed back into themselves: an error stored this step is read next step and smoothed into the next value.
items.deeper_md:
The quantities first: both moments at about 1.0625 bytes per parameter on eligible tensors against 8 bytes in FP32, a 7.53× compression, roughly 19.2 GB of persistent state for the 2.7B pretraining run. The preconditioner is defined as h_t(v) = 1/(√(v/(1−β₂ᵗ)) + ε), and the argument is local: for the quantisation cell adjacent to zero, small average error in v does not imply small average error in h_t at the next step. Two recipes follow. ZIP-SR keeps zero in the second-moment codebook and computes stochastic-rounding probabilities in preconditioner space; ZE-EDEN drops zero and rescales each quantised block to undo the distortion the positive floor introduces. Both use NF4 for the first moment, whose block-normalised reconstruction error measured 1.056 × 10⁻³ against 1.739 × 10⁻³ for FP4.

Validation-loss gaps to 32-bit AdamW, mean of three paired seeds at 20 tokens per parameter on FineWeb-Edu: GPT-1.4B moves from +0.0521 under TorchAO's 4-bit AdamW to +0.0156 under ZIP-SR, which is the 70 percent figure; Llama-1.1B from +0.0486 to +0.0198. At GPT-2.7B TorchAO diverges late in cooldown at +1.5435 while ZIP-SR holds +0.0343, so no percentage is quoted there.

The authors' own limits: the theory is a one-step bias analysis plus a one-dimensional quadratic toy problem, not an end-to-end convergence result; the directional first-moment bias they patch with stochastic rounding over the last 10 percent of training is unexplained; and nothing below 4 bits or outside AdamW was tested.

glossary.definition: Adam's exponentially smoothed average of squared gradients, kept per parameter; it enters the update only as 1/√v, which is why its absolute value matters less than that reciprocal.
The per-parameter factor an adaptive optimiser multiplies the gradient by before stepping; in Adam it is 1/(√v + ε), so it shrinks steps for parameters with noisy histories.
Rounding up or down at random with probability set by how close the value sits to each level, so the error has zero mean and does not accumulate over many updates the way nearest-rounding does.
4-bit NormalFloat — a 16-level codebook placed at quantiles of a normal distribution rather than uniformly, including an exact zero, built for weights that are approximately Gaussian within a block.

foundations.subtitle: Hot potassium hydroxide dissolves silicon hundreds of times faster in some directions than others, so a beaker and a hard mask can cut a wall at exactly 54.74°.
foundations.tldr: Hot potassium hydroxide dissolves silicon, but not at the same speed in every direction: the most tightly bonded atomic planes resist it by a factor of a hundred or more. Mask a (100) wafer, drop it in the bath, and the etch digs down until those slow planes are exposed, then effectively stops widening — leaving a groove whose walls sit at 54.74° whether you etch for ten minutes or an hour. The shape comes from the crystal, not from the tool, which is why a process with no vacuum chamber and no plasma can still hold a dimension.

sections.heading: A beaker should not be able to make a straight wall
sections.body_md:
Start with what wet chemistry normally does to a solid. Dissolution is a surface reaction, and a surface reaction that proceeds at the same rate everywhere eats a hemisphere out of a masked opening: the etch front moves sideways under the mask exactly as fast as it moves down. That is isotropic etching, and it is why a hydrofluoric–nitric mixture can thin a wafer but cannot define a trench. Depth and undercut are the same number, so the aspect ratio of anything you make is fixed at roughly one, and the mask edge stops being a dimension.

Silicon in hot alkali breaks that rule. The dissolution rate depends on which crystal plane is exposed, and the dependence is enormous: ratios between the fast {100} planes and the slow {111} planes are a hundred to one or higher. The consequence is geometric rather than chemical. Whatever shape you start with, the etch quickly exposes the slowest-etching planes available, and from then on the slow planes are the walls. The bath stops being a subtractive tool and becomes a device that reveals a shape already present in the lattice.
sections.deeper_md: The isotropic case is not useless, it is just differently useful: a hydrofluoric–nitric–acetic mixture is the standard way to round a sharp corner, remove saw damage, or delineate a junction, precisely because it does not care about orientation. The practical consequence of isotropy is that the lateral etch under a mask is approximately equal to the etch depth, so a 10 µm deep pocket arrives with about 10 µm of undercut on every side and the mask opening has to be drawn smaller than the feature by that amount.

sections.heading: Why the (111) plane holds out
sections.body_md:
Cut a diamond-lattice crystal along (111) and every surface atom has three of its four bonds pointing down into the crystal and one pointing up out of it. Cut along (100) and each surface atom has two of each. The {111} planes are the most densely packed, so they present the fewest bonds an etchant can reach, and removing one atom from them means breaking three bonds to the bulk rather than two.

Seidel and co-authors turned that counting into an electrochemical model in 1990, and it is still the one quoted. Four hydroxide ions oxidise a single surface silicon atom and inject four electrons into the conduction band; the step that limits the rate is breaking the backbonds, which requires thermally exciting the electrons in those backbond surface states up into the conduction band. The injected electrons then reduce water, regenerating hydroxide and releasing hydrogen, and the silicon leaves as monosilicic acid, Si(OH)₄. Anisotropy, in this account, is not a large difference in anything — it is a small difference in the energy of the backbond surface states from one orientation to the next, amplified by an exponential. Slowly etching planes show the higher activation energies, exactly as that story requires.
sections.deeper_md: Two features of Seidel's model are worth sitting with, because they explain things a bond count alone does not. First, it is electrochemical rather than simple acid–base: four electrons are injected into the conduction band and later consumed reducing water, so the same reaction that dissolves the silicon regenerates its own hydroxide. That closed loop is why the species in the balance sheet is water and not hydroxide. Second, the rate-limiting step is thermal excitation of a backbond surface state, which means the orientation dependence enters as an activation energy rather than as a pre-factor — Seidel reports slowly etching planes measuring the higher activation energies in the same experiment. An exponential of a small energy difference is how a difference the model itself calls small produces a rate ratio in the hundreds.

sections.heading: The geometry does the dimensioning
sections.body_md:
On a (100) wafer the {111} planes intersect the surface at 54.74°, and that angle is set by the lattice, not by the recipe. Open a square window in a hard mask with its edges parallel to the wafer's primary flat, and the etch sinks a pit with four sloping walls. Two things follow, and they are the reason this process survives.

First, the pit is self-limiting in depth. The two opposing walls converge, and for an opening of width W they meet at a depth of W/√2, about 0.707 W — so a 100 µm opening bottoms out near 71 µm and then essentially stops. Etch time stops being a dimension; mask width becomes one. Second, the sidewall angle is a constant you can design against, which is why this is still how fibre-alignment V-grooves and silicon nozzle plates get made.

Change the wafer and you change the geometry rather than the chemistry. On a (110) wafer the {111} planes stand perpendicular to the surface, so the same bath cuts vertical-walled trenches. The trade is supply: (110) wafers are less common and more expensive than (100).
sections.deeper_md: Work the depth arithmetic through, because it is the part that does real design work. The walls make an angle θ = 54.74° with the surface, so each wall advances inward by its depth times cot θ; two walls closing from opposite sides of an opening W meet when 2·d·cot(54.74°) = W, and cot(54.74°) = 1/√2, giving d = W/√2. Everything a (100) alkaline etch can make is therefore a function of mask width: a window narrower than √2 times the wafer thickness ends as a sealed V, a wider one breaks through as a membrane or a hole, and the crossover is a line you can draw before you own a bath. The angle also sets the price of the process: a through-etch of a 500 µm wafer loses about 354 µm of lateral space on every side, which is why wet-etched features are large even when the lithography is not.

sections.heading: More hydroxide is not more etching
sections.body_md:
Here is the result that catches people. MIT's teaching wet station lists 20 % KOH at 80 °C etching silicon at 85 µm per hour. UBC's recipe — 70 g of KOH pellets in 190 ml of deionised water, about 30 %, also at 80 °C — is quoted at roughly 1 µm per minute, which is 60 µm per hour. Two different labs, two different concentrations, and the more concentrated bath is the slower one.

The reason is in Seidel's model. Hydroxide does the oxidising, but water is what the injected electrons reduce, and in a concentrated alkali solution water is the species in short supply. Seidel reports the rate tracking the fourth power of water concentration in concentrated KOH, which makes dilution a far more sensitive knob than intuition suggests: raise the water content by a tenth and the fourth power turns that into about 1.46 times the rate. Temperature matters too, through the activation energy, but concentration is the lever that surprises.

Isopropanol is the other common addition, 40 ml in the UBC recipe. It slows the etch and increases the anisotropy, which is the trade a smooth {111} sidewall is usually worth.
sections.deeper_md: The fourth-power dependence is also a uniformity problem, because water is consumed and hydrogen is evolved: a long etch in a small, unstirred bath drifts in concentration and therefore in rate, and the evolved hydrogen bubbles stick to the surface and mask it locally, which is one origin of the hillocks that make a KOH-etched floor rough. Stirring addresses both. Note that the two rate figures above come from two institutions' process sheets rather than from one controlled experiment, so read them as the right order of magnitude and the right direction, not as a measured concentration curve.

sections.heading: The mask, and the potassium problem
sections.body_md:
Photoresist does not survive this. The bath is a strong base at 80 °C, so the pattern has to be transferred into a hard mask first — thermal oxide or, better, silicon nitride. KOH etches silicon dioxide slowly but not negligibly, so for a deep etch nitride is the standard choice; UBC specifies 2000–3000 Å of either. Doping gives you a second kind of stop: the etch rate is independent of arsenic, phosphorus and antimony concentration, but heavy boron slows it sharply, which is how a buried p⁺ layer becomes a membrane of defined thickness.

The constraint that keeps KOH out of most CMOS lines is not chemical but contamination. Potassium is a mobile alkali ion: get it into a gate oxide and it drifts under bias, shifting threshold voltage over the life of the part. MIT's process sheet handles this administratively rather than chemically — KOH work uses separately coloured labware, and a wafer that has been in the bath needs a double piranha clean before it is allowed back into the main line. Tetramethylammonium hydroxide is the metal-free substitute, listed at 25 % and 80 °C for 20 µm per hour: a third of KOH's rate, slightly lower anisotropy, rougher floors, and allowed near transistors.
sections.deeper_md: The oxide-versus-nitride decision is a selectivity calculation, not a preference. If the mask etches at rate r_m and the silicon at rate r_s, a target depth d consumes d·(r_m/r_s) of mask, so the mask thickness you need scales with the depth you want — which is exactly why a thin thermal oxide is fine for a 5 µm pocket and useless for a through-wafer etch. TMAH's much higher selectivity to oxide is the reason it is often chosen even where potassium would be tolerated: a patterned oxide you already have can serve as the mask with no extra deposition step.

sections.heading: What it is still for
sections.body_md:
Anisotropic wet etching is not a legacy process. NIST's NanoFab runs a dedicated Reynolds Tech silicon etch bench with a 45 % KOH dip tank, heated deionised water and hydrochloric acid, handling wafers up to 200 mm, and lists its purposes plainly: opening windows in silicon to form membranes, and shaping silicon parts for microelectromechanical systems. That is the enduring niche — anything where the thing you want is a hole all the way through, or a thin suspended plate, or a precisely angled facet.

The reason it has not been replaced by deep reactive-ion etching is throughput and cost. A wet bath processes a whole carrier of wafers at once, needs no vacuum, no plasma source and no fluorine chemistry, and holds its dimension from the lattice rather than from a tuned recipe. Deep RIE gives vertical walls on any wafer orientation and any mask shape, which wet etching cannot, and it leaves scalloped sidewalls and costs a tool. For a V-groove, a pyramidal pit, or a 200-wafer batch of membranes, a hot beaker is still the better engineering answer.
sections.deeper_md:
The largest application by area in the world is the one nobody files under MEMS: the pyramid texture on the front of a monocrystalline solar cell is this same etch, run dilute. PV-Manufacturing.org gives 1–2 % KOH at 70–80 °C and a rate held at or below 2 µm/min to keep it anisotropic, producing pyramids with 5–6 µm base edges — optimal range 3–10 µm — at close to full coverage, and isopropanol is in the bath as a surfactant to let the evolved hydrogen bubbles detach rather than micromask the surface into round hillocks.

The interesting part is that the facet angle does not come out at 54.74°. The same source notes industrial texturing lands at 49–53°, because the pyramid tips spend the longest in the etch. Baker-Finch and McIntosh pushed this further in 2013: they argue {111}-faceted pyramids are a poor description of real textured silicon, that the features are hillocks with an octagonal base and a characteristic base angle nearer 50–52°, and that a higher base angle lowers hemispherical reflectance. Their own accounting makes the cost small once an antireflection coating is present — about 0.2 % of photogenerated current for a 50° hillock morphology against ideal {111} pyramids — which is why the simple model survives in process literature despite being wrong about the geometry.

glossary.definition: A notation for crystal planes: the numbers are the reciprocals of where the plane cuts the crystal axes. Curly braces, {111}, mean the whole family of planes equivalent by symmetry.

An etch whose rate depends on direction. In wet silicon etching the direction that matters is the crystal orientation of the exposed surface; in plasma etching it is the direction of ion bombardment, which is a different mechanism with the same name.

A bond from a surface atom down into the bulk crystal rather than out into the ambient. A (111) surface silicon atom has three of them and a (100) atom two, and breaking them is the rate-limiting step in alkaline etching.

A patterned inorganic film — thermal oxide or silicon nitride — used where photoresist would be destroyed or undercut. Its required thickness is set by its own etch rate times the depth you want in the substrate.

A layer or condition that slows the etch to near zero so the process self-terminates at a known depth. Here it is heavy boron doping, which drops the silicon etch rate sharply and leaves a membrane of the doped thickness.

A small residual pyramid left standing on a nominally flat etched floor, usually nucleated by a hydrogen bubble or a micromask that locally protected the surface; it is the main surface-quality complaint against TMAH.

foundations.try_this: Mix the UBC recipe — 70 g of KOH pellets in 190 ml of deionised water with 40 ml of isopropanol — hold it at 80 °C on a hot plate with a face shield and base-rated gloves, dip a bare (100) test piece in dilute HF first to clear the native oxide, then etch for twenty minutes. Weigh the piece before and after on the lab balance and convert mass loss to thickness using silicon's 2.33 g/cm³ and the measured area of the piece, remembering that both faces and all four edges are etching: you should land near 1 µm/min. Then predict, in writing and before you run it, which direction the rate moves if you halve the KOH concentration — MIT's wet station lists 20 % KOH at 85 µm/hour and UBC lists 30 % at about 60, and Seidel's fourth-power water dependence is why. Keep the KOH labware permanently separate from anything that will go back into the oxidation furnace.
